newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Nominees of Central African mutineers in cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Nominees of Central African mutineers in cabinet.

text.p: Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse has given two government posts to nominees of former army mutineers as part of reconciliation measures following a series of bloody army revolts.
Residents reported an exchange of fire in the capital overnight between local soldiers and African peacekeepers but had no immediate explanation. There were no casualties.
The appointments, announced on state television on Monday night, followed talks earlier in the day between Patasse and leaders of troops who mutinied three times in less than a year.
"The people of Central African Republic are marching towards national reconciliation," Patasse said at the meeting, the second this month with the former rebels.
"Our first meeting did not only reinstill a feeling of patriotism among our people, but also a return to confidence among foreign investors," Patasse said at the talks.
Presidential spokesman Prosper Ndouba said former interior minister Lieutenant-Colonel Evariste Martial Konzale had been put in charge of security and disarming civilians.
Brigadier-General Didas Ndayen, a former secretary of state for defence, was given the job of reorganising the army.
They will have the rank of minister-delegate. Demobilisation, redeployment and reincorporation into civilian life would be offered to the soldiers with United Nations help.

Captain Anicet Caulet, rebel spokesman at the height of the revolt, led the ex-rebels at the meeting. Also present was former Malian military ruler General Amadou Toumani Toure, who is overseeing a regional peace plan that ended the unrest.
Patasse urged the soldiers to start disarmament of and a return to barracks of mutinous soldiers as agreed in the plan.
A March 31 disarmament deadline was extended after African peacekeepers and army mutineers and their supporters clashed on March 22 and 23. At least five people were killed.

The clashes were the worst since Patasse and his rivals agreed the African-mediated peace plan in January. The mutineers, from the southern Yakoma tribe, rejected a Patasse amnesty linked to disarmament.
The first mutinies last April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a northern civilian who won 1993 presidential elections.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic bloodshed. French troops, in the country under a defence pact, restored order and handed over to peacekeepers.
